content: Venice treacle, also known as Andromachi theriaca, Theriacum Andromachi, or the treacle of Andromachus, was a medicinal preparation historically used as an antidote to venom. It was a complex compound, primarily based on honey or molasses, and was first formulated in Italy before being widely distributed across Europe, particularly from Venice. The formulation of this theriac, as recorded in the 1686 d'Amsterdammer Apotheek, included a wide array of ingredients, categorized as roots, leaves, flowers, seeds, and other substances. The following is a detailed breakdown of its components: Roots: Iris: Likely referring to the rhizome of the iris plant, used for its aromatic and medicinal properties. Balsamorhiza deltoidea: Known for its potential anti-inflammatory effects. Potentilla reptans (creeping cinquefoil): Traditionally used for its astringent properties. Rheum rhabarbarum (garden rhubarb): Valued for its purgative and digestive benefits. Zingiber (ginger): Known for its anti-inflammatory and digestive properties. Angustafolia odorata: Likely a fragrant root with medicinal uses. Gentiana (gentian): Used to stimulate appetite and aid digestion. Meum athamanticum (spignel): A plant with aromatic and carminative properties. Valeriana (valerian): Known for its sedative effects. Corydalis cava (hollowroot): Traditionally used for pain relief. Agaricus: Likely referring to a type of fungus with medicinal uses. Cinnamomum zeylanicum (cinnamon) and Cinnamomum aromaticum (cassia): Both used for their warming and aromatic properties. Leaves: Teucrium scordium (water germander): Historically used for its antiseptic properties. Fraxinus excelsior (ash): Known for its diuretic and anti-inflammatory effects. Clinopodium calamintha (lesser calamint): Used for its aromatic and digestive benefits. Marrubium vulgare (white horehound): A traditional remedy for respiratory conditions. Cymbopogon citratus (lemongrass): Known for its calming and digestive properties. Teucrium chamaedrys (wall germander): Used for its tonic and astringent effects. Cupressaceae: Likely referring to plants in the cypress family, used for their aromatic and medicinal properties. Laurus nobilis (bay laurel): Known for its aromatic and digestive benefits. Polium montanum: A plant with potential medicinal uses. Piper nigrum (black pepper) and Piper longum (long pepper): Both used for their warming and digestive properties. Juniperus (juniper): Known for its diuretic and antiseptic effects. Syzygium aromaticum (clove): Used for its analgesic and aromatic properties. Flowers: Rosa (rose): Valued for its aromatic and astringent properties. Crocus sativus (saffron): Known for its anti-inflammatory and mood-enhancing effects. Lavandula stoechas (French lavender): Used for its calming and antiseptic properties. Centaurium minoris: Likely referring to a plant with bitter and tonic properties. Seeds: Brassica napus (rapeseed): Used for its oil and potential medicinal properties. Petroselinum (parsley): Known for its diuretic and digestive benefits. Nigella sativa (black seed): Valued for its anti-inflammatory and immune-boosting effects. Pimpinella anisum (anise): Used for its carminative and digestive properties. Elettaria cardamomum (cardamom): Known for its aromatic and digestive benefits. Foeniculum vulgare (fennel): Used for its carminative and digestive properties. Hypericum perforatum (St. John’s wort): Known for its antidepressant and anti-inflammatory effects. Seseli: Likely referring to a plant with medicinal uses. Thlaspi: A plant with potential therapeutic properties. Daucus carota (carrot): Used for its nutritional and medicinal benefits. Lavandula angustifolia (common lavender): Known for its calming and antiseptic properties. Papaver somniferum (opium poppy): Used historically for its analgesic and sedative effects. Glycyrrhiza (licorice): Valued for its anti-inflammatory and soothing properties. Cytinus hypocistis: A parasitic plant with potential medicinal uses. Acaciae (acacia): Used for its astringent and soothing properties. Styrax benzoin (benzoin): Known for its aromatic and antiseptic effects. Gummi arabicum (gum arabic): Used as a binder and emulsifier in medicinal preparations. Sagapeni: Likely a resin from an unknown tree, possibly a type of Ferula. Gummi Opopanax chironium and Gummi Ferula foetida: Resins with potential medicinal uses. Dead Sea bitumen: A mineral substance with historical medicinal applications. Commiphora (myrrh): Known for its antiseptic and anti-inflammatory properties. Incense: Used for its aromatic and potential therapeutic effects. Turpentine from Cyprus: Historically used for its antiseptic properties. Boli armen Verae: Likely a type of red clay with medicinal uses. Chalciditis: A copper-containing substance with potential therapeutic applications. Castoreum: A secretion from beavers, historically used for its antispasmodic properties. Oil from Myristica fragrans (nutmeg): Known for its warming and digestive benefits. Trochisci Viperarum: Likely a preparation involving viper flesh or venom, used in traditional medicine. Magmatis Hedychroi: Possibly a fragrant or medicinal preparation. Canary Island wine: Used as a solvent or preservative. Narbonne white honey: Valued for its sweetness and preservative properties. This intricate combination of ingredients reflects the historical complexity of medicinal formulations and the belief in the synergistic effects of multiple substances to combat venom and other ailments.
